Unit I: Fundamentals & Bootstrapping CO1

Deep Dive: Process State Transition stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> New New --> Ready : Admitted Ready --> Running : Scheduler Dispatch Running --> Ready : Interrupt Running --> Waiting : I/O or Event Wait Waiting --> Ready : I/O or Event Completion Running --> Terminated : Exit Terminated --> [*] Context Switching: Saving the state of a PCB (Program Control Block) and loading a new one. It is pure overhead, no useful work gets done. Paging vs Segmentation: Paging divides memory into fixed-size blocks (pages/frames) eliminating external fragmentation. Segmentation divides memory into variable-sized logical blocks (functions, objects) avoiding internal fragmentation. TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer): A hardware cache for the page table. A TLB hit avoids the slow memory access required to look up a page frame.

Deep Dive: Concurrency & Traps Deadlocks (Banker's Algorithm): Avoids deadlocks by simulating the allocation of predetermined maximum possible amounts of all resources, and checks if the system remains in a "safe state". Belady's Anomaly: Increasing the number of page frames results in an INCREASE in page faults. Occurs strictly with FIFO page replacement. Priority Inversion: A low priority task holds a lock needed by a high priority task, but a medium priority task preempts the low one, blocking the high priority task forever. Fix: Priority Inheritance. Thrashing: CPU utilization drops to 0% because processes spend all their time swapping pages to disk instead of executing.

System Calls & Interrupts A system call transitions the CPU from user mode to kernel mode via a software interrupt (trap). It provides controlled access to protected OS services. An interrupt vector table routes execution to the correct handler routine in memory. Example: fork() triggering a 0x80 instruction in x86 architectures.

Dual-Mode Operation Hardware support ensures isolation. Mode bit (0=Kernel, 1=User) prevents user code from executing privileged instructions (e.g., halting CPU, memory mapping). Timer interrupts forcibly return control to the OS. Example: A user program trying to execute a CLI (clear interrupts) instruction triggers a protection fault. Examiner Trap: Distinguish between a hardware interrupt (asynchronous external signal) and a trap (synchronous software-generated exception).

OS Kernel Architectures Monolithic: Entire OS runs in kernel space (Linux). High throughput, but bugs crash the system. Microkernel: Only bare essentials (IPC, basic scheduling) run in kernel space; rest in user space (Mach, QNX). Highly resilient but IPC overhead limits speed. Example: Linux kernel panics due to a faulty GPU driver, whereas QNX just restarts the driver service. Pro-Tip: Hybrid kernels (Windows NT, macOS XNU) dynamically load modules into a monolithic core, combining both approaches.
Unit II: Process Management & Threads CO2

Process State Transitions Processes migrate through queues. Context Switching saves the current Process Control Block (PCB) and loads the next. It is pure overhead where no useful computation occurs. Example: Process waits on read() , moving from Running to Blocked state. stateDiagram-v2 New --> Ready: Admitted Ready --> Running: Dispatched Running --> Ready: Interrupt/Preempt Running --> Blocked: I/O Request Blocked --> Ready: I/O Complete Running --> Terminated: Exit

CPU Scheduling Tactics SJF (Shortest Job First): Provably optimal for average waiting time, but risks starvation. Round Robin (RR): Time-slices (quanta) prevent starvation; heavily relies on quantum length tuning. Example: A 10ms quantum in RR perfectly balances responsiveness for interactive tasks against context-switching overhead. Examiner Trap: Non-preemptive SJF vs. Preemptive SRTF (Shortest Remaining Time First). SRTF recalculates burst times dynamically.

Multithreading Models Many-to-One: Thread library maps multiple user threads to one kernel thread. Fast but blocks the entire process if one thread blocks. One-to-One: Direct mapping (Linux, Windows). High concurrency but high kernel overhead. Example: A Web server using One-to-One threading can still serve requests if one thread blocks on disk I/O.
Unit III: Concurrency & Deadlocks CO3

Critical Section & Semaphores A critical section requires Mutual Exclusion, Progress, and Bounded Waiting . Semaphores are integer variables accessed via atomic wait(P) and signal(V) operations to orchestrate access. Example: Using a counting semaphore initialized to 5 to restrict maximum concurrent database connections. Examiner Trap: A Mutex is NOT just a binary semaphore. Mutexes have ownership; only the locking thread can unlock. Semaphores can be signaled by any thread.

Priority Inversion & Inheritance Occurs when a lower-priority task holds a lock needed by a higher-priority task, while a medium-priority task preempts the low one, effectively starving the high-priority task. Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP) temporarily boosts the lower task's priority. Example: The Mars Pathfinder rover resetting due to priority inversion on the data bus mutex.

Deadlock Characterization Requires four simultaneous conditions: Mutual Exclusion, Hold & Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait. Banker's Algorithm statically analyzes max resource claims to ensure the system remains in a "safe state". Example: A safe sequence <P1, P3, P2> guarantees all processes can finish without deadlocking. graph LR P1((Process 1)) -->|Requests| R1[Resource A] R1 -->|Assigned to| P2((Process 2)) P2 -->|Requests| R2[Resource B] R2 -->|Assigned to| P1 Pro-Tip: The Ostrich Algorithm (ignoring deadlocks entirely) is actively used by Linux/Windows due to the high overhead of continuous prevention.
Unit IV: Memory Management CO4

Paging & Translation Lookaside Buffer Memory is divided into fixed-size frames (physical) and pages (logical), eliminating external fragmentation. The TLB is a fast associative cache mapping virtual pages to physical frames, drastically reducing the latency of a two-step memory access. Example: A TLB hit allows direct memory access; a miss requires traversing the hierarchical page table in main memory. Examiner Trap: Internal fragmentation is still possible in paging if a process doesn't exactly fill its final allocated frame.

Virtual Memory & Demand Paging Creates an illusion of continuous memory exceeding physical RAM. Pages are lazily loaded on a Page Fault . If RAM is full, a victim page is swapped to disk. Example: Opening a 10GB video file on a machine with 4GB RAM by mapping only the active chunks.

Thrashing & Belady's Anomaly Thrashing happens when the system spends more time swapping pages than executing code. Cured by adjusting the Working Set. Belady's Anomaly is a counterintuitive phenomenon where adding more frames increases page faults. Example: FIFO replacement suffering Belady's Anomaly on the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .
Unit V: Storage & File Systems CO5

Disk Scheduling Algorithms Minimizing head movement (seek time) is critical. SSTF picks the closest request but starves distant ones. C-SCAN (Circular Elevator) moves the head continuously from inner to outer tracks, providing uniform wait times. Example: C-SCAN servicing cylinders in the sequence: 10, 30, 90, 150, 199, 0, 5 .

File System Structures (Inodes) Unix Inodes separate metadata (permissions, sizes, timestamps) from actual data blocks. They use direct, single, double, and triple indirect pointers to accommodate massive files without bloating the inode table. Example: A 10GB file utilizing a double-indirect pointer, traversing two pointer blocks before hitting the actual data block. flowchart LR Inode --> Direct[Direct Blocks] Inode --> Single[Single Indirect] Single --> Blocks[Data Blocks] Inode --> Double[Double Indirect] Examiner Trap: Inodes do NOT store the file name. The directory structure maps file names to inode numbers.

Direct Memory Access (DMA) A specialized hardware controller takes over the system bus to transfer massive data blocks directly between an I/O device and RAM, bypassing the CPU to prevent cycle stealing. Example: A Gigabit network card writing incoming packets directly to a buffer in RAM while the CPU continues executing a game. ﻿
Applied Examples & Important Concepts

Define Operating System. An Operating System (OS) is system software that acts as an intermediary between computer hardware and the computer user. It manages hardware resources and provides common services for computer programs, ensuring efficient and convenient execution of user applications.

List any four functions of an Operating System. Process Management: Scheduling and execution of processes. Memory Management: Allocation and de-allocation of memory space. File Management: Organizing and tracking files and directories. Device/I/O Management: Managing device drivers and hardware communication.

What is the Mode Bit? What do the values 0 and 1 represent? The Mode Bit is a hardware flag used by the OS to differentiate between user-level and system-level execution to protect system integrity. 0: Kernel Mode (System/Supervisor mode) - full access to hardware. 1: User Mode - restricted access.

Differentiate between User Mode and Kernel Mode. User Mode (Mode bit = 1) Kernel Mode (Mode bit = 0) Restricted access to memory and hardware. Direct access to all memory and hardware. Cannot execute privileged instructions. Can execute any CPU instruction. Application programs run here. Core OS components run here.

What is the difference between Hardware Interrupts and Software Interrupts? Hardware Interrupts are asynchronous signals generated by external hardware devices (e.g., keyboard press, disk I/O completion) to get the CPU's attention. Software Interrupts (Traps) are synchronous signals generated by executing instructions within a program (e.g., system calls, division by zero errors).

A student's program gets stuck in an infinite loop. Which OS mechanism ensures the system does not freeze permanently, and how? The Timer (Hardware Timer) mechanism prevents permanent freezing. The OS sets a timer to interrupt the CPU after a specific time slice (quantum). When the timer expires, it generates an interrupt that forces the CPU back into Kernel Mode, allowing the OS to regain control and forcefully terminate or preempt the looping program.

Explain, in brief, why a Monolithic OS structure is fast but hard to maintain, whereas a Microkernel structure is more reliable but comparatively slower. A Monolithic OS bundles all services (file system, drivers, memory) into a single large kernel, making execution fast (no message passing overhead) but hard to maintain due to tight coupling. A Microkernel keeps only essential services in the kernel and runs the rest in user space; this is reliable (a failed driver won't crash the OS) but slower due to the overhead of inter-process communication (IPC) and frequent mode switching.

Define Batch Operating System and mention one limitation of this type of system. A Batch Operating System groups similar jobs into "batches" and executes them sequentially without manual intervention. Users submit jobs to an operator, who batches them and feeds them to the computer. Limitation: Lack of user interaction. Once a job is submitted, the user must wait for it to finish; if it enters an infinite loop or requires input, the CPU may idle, and debugging is extremely difficult.

What are System Calls? List any three categories of System Calls. System Calls provide the programming interface between a user application and the operating system services. They act as a bridge allowing user programs to request privileged operations (like reading a file) from the OS kernel. Categories: Process Control: fork() , exit() File Management: open() , read() , write() Device Management: ioctl() , read() from device

Differentiate between Multiprogramming Operating System and Time-Sharing Operating System. Multiprogramming OS Time-Sharing OS Goal: Maximize CPU utilization by keeping the CPU busy. Goal: Maximize user responsiveness and interactivity. Switches jobs only when the current job waits for I/O. Switches jobs frequently based on a time quantum (timer). Users cannot interact with programs during execution. Multiple users can interact with the system simultaneously.

Explain the working of Interrupt-Driven I/O and state why it is more efficient than Programmed I/O. In Interrupt-Driven I/O , the CPU issues an I/O command to a device controller and immediately resumes executing other tasks. When the device controller finishes reading/writing the data, it sends a hardware interrupt to the CPU. The CPU briefly pauses its current work, processes the data, and resumes. Efficiency: It eliminates "busy waiting" (polling). The CPU does not waste cycles constantly checking if the device is ready, allowing for true concurrent execution.

Compare Single-Processor Systems and Multiprocessor Systems on the basis of number of CPUs, coupling, and reliability. Feature Single-Processor Multiprocessor Number of CPUs Only one main CPU. Two or more CPUs sharing memory. Coupling N/A (Standalone). Tightly coupled (share clock and memory). Reliability Low (If CPU fails, system halts). High (Graceful degradation; if one fails, others take over).

A hospital requires a system where every task must be completed within a strict deadline, or the result is considered useless even if computed correctly. Identify the suitable type of Operating System for this requirement and justify your answer. A Hard Real-Time Operating System is required. Justification: Hard real-time systems guarantee that critical tasks complete on time. In a hospital (e.g., a pacemaker or life-support system), missing a deadline can result in death. Other OS types like Time-Sharing prioritize fairness over strict deadlines, which would be fatal here.

Trace the sequence of steps that occur when a user application issues a request to read a file from the disk, starting from the System Call up to the return of control to the user program. The user application makes a read() System Call . The CPU switches to Kernel Mode via a software trap. The OS asks the Device Controller (disk) to fetch the file. The CPU switches to another process while waiting (Interrupt-driven I/O). The disk finishes and sends a Hardware Interrupt to the CPU. The OS copies the data into the user program's memory. The OS switches back to User Mode and returns control to the application.

Justify why modern Operating Systems such as Linux use a Module-Based structure instead of a purely Monolithic or purely Microkernel structure. Support your answer with suitable advantages. Modern systems use a Hybrid / Loadable Kernel Module (LKM) structure to get the best of both worlds: Performance (Like Monolithic): Modules are loaded directly into the kernel space, meaning there is no slow message-passing overhead like in Microkernels. Flexibility (Like Microkernel): The core kernel remains small. Device drivers and file systems can be loaded dynamically at runtime without rebooting the system or recompiling the entire monolithic kernel.

Explain the Dual-Mode operation of an Operating System. How do the Mode Bit and the Timer mechanism work together to protect the system? Dual-Mode Operation provides hardware-level protection by dividing execution into User Mode (Bit=1) and Kernel Mode (Bit=0). Privileged instructions (like halting the CPU or direct hardware I/O) can only execute in Kernel Mode. How they work together: If a malicious user program runs in User Mode, it cannot directly crash the hardware because it lacks privileges. However, it could write an infinite loop to hog the CPU forever. This is where the Timer steps in. The OS configures the hardware timer before switching to User Mode. When the timer hits zero, it triggers an interrupt. The hardware forces the mode bit to 0 (Kernel Mode) and hands control back to the OS, which can then safely kill the malicious looping program.

Compare and contrast Programmed I/O, Interrupt-Driven I/O, and Direct Memory Access (DMA) in terms of CPU involvement and overall system efficiency. Method CPU Involvement System Efficiency Programmed I/O Extremely High. CPU must manually check device status (polling) and transfer every byte. Very Low. CPU wastes cycles busy-waiting instead of running logic. Interrupt-Driven I/O Moderate. CPU issues command and leaves, but must still handle an interrupt for every single byte/word transferred. Better. CPU can do other work, but heavy I/O causes too many interrupts, slowing it down. DMA Very Low. CPU only issues the start command. DMA controller moves entire blocks of data. CPU interrupted only once at the end. Highest. CPU is fully freed to execute heavy processes concurrently with I/O.

A university wants to set up a computer lab where many students run their programs at the same time, each getting a quick, fair share of CPU time so the system feels interactive to everyone. Suggest a suitable type of Operating System and justify your answer. The suitable OS is a Time-Sharing Operating System . Justification: Time-Sharing is designed specifically for interactivity among multiple users. It uses CPU scheduling and multiprogramming to provide each user with a small portion of a time-shared computer. The CPU switches from one student's program to the next extremely rapidly (e.g., every 100 milliseconds). Because the switching is so fast, every student gets immediate response times and feels as though they have their own dedicated computer, satisfying the "interactive" and "fair share" requirements.

A company's server crashes frequently because a bug in a single device driver brings down the entire kernel, since the system uses a Monolithic structure. As an OS designer, propose a better structural approach to avoid this problem, and explain the trade-offs of your proposed solution. Proposed Solution: A Microkernel Architecture . By moving the device drivers out of the privileged kernel space and running them as standard user-level processes, a bug or crash in the device driver will only kill that specific process. The Microkernel itself remains isolated and untouched, meaning the server will not crash. Trade-offs: The primary disadvantage is Performance Overhead . Because the driver is now in user space, communicating with it requires Inter-Process Communication (IPC) and constant context switching between User Mode and Kernel Mode, which slows the system down compared to the direct function calls of a Monolithic kernel.

Trace a complete scenario: a user clicks 'Print' on a document. Explain, step by step, the roles of the System Call, Device Controller, Interrupt Mechanism, and the switching between User Mode and Kernel Mode in completing this print operation. The Word processor (in User Mode ) issues a write() System Call to send data to the printer. A trap occurs, changing the mode bit to 0, switching execution to Kernel Mode . The OS kernel verifies permissions and sends the print command to the Printer's Device Controller . The OS puts the Word processor in a waiting state and switches the CPU back to User Mode to run other programs while the printer works. The Printer Controller prints the page. Once finished, it sends a Hardware Interrupt to the CPU. The CPU switches back to Kernel Mode , processes the interrupt, and marks the Word processor as ready to resume. The OS switches back to User Mode and control returns to Word, notifying the user it finished.

Define a Process. How is a process different from a program? A Process is a program in execution. It is an active entity. Difference: A program is a passive entity (a file containing code stored on disk). A process is active; it has a program counter specifying the next instruction to execute, and associated resources (memory, registers).

What is a Process Control Block (PCB)? A Process Control Block (PCB) is a data structure in the OS kernel containing all the information needed to manage a specific process. It acts as the repository for any information that may vary from process to process (e.g., process state, program counter, CPU registers, memory limits).

Define Context Switching. Context Switching is the mechanism where the OS saves the state (context) of the currently running process into its PCB and loads the saved state of another process from its PCB, allowing the CPU to switch execution from one process to another seamlessly.

Differentiate between a User Thread and a Kernel Thread. User Thread Kernel Thread Managed by a user-level thread library. Managed directly by the OS kernel. OS is unaware of them. If one blocks, the whole process blocks. OS is aware. If one blocks, OS can schedule another thread in the same process. Fast context switching (no OS intervention). Slower context switching (requires Kernel Mode).

A process is running on the CPU when a timer interrupt occurs. Name the mechanism the OS uses at this moment to switch to another process. The mechanism is Context Switching , initiated by the Short-Term Scheduler (CPU Scheduler) and executed by the Dispatcher .

List and briefly explain the five states in the process life cycle. New: The process is being created. Ready: The process is waiting to be assigned to a processor. Running: Instructions are being executed on the CPU. Waiting (Blocked): The process is waiting for some event to occur (e.g., I/O completion). Terminated: The process has finished execution.

Explain any three attributes stored in a Process Control Block (PCB). Process State: The current status of the process (New, Ready, Running, Waiting). Program Counter: The memory address of the very next instruction the CPU must execute for this process. CPU Registers: Saves the contents of accumulators, index registers, and general-purpose registers so execution can resume seamlessly after an interrupt.

List the three types of process schedulers and state the function of each. Long-Term Scheduler (Job Scheduler): Selects processes from the disk and loads them into memory for execution, controlling the Degree of Multiprogramming. Short-Term Scheduler (CPU Scheduler): Selects a process from the Ready Queue and allocates the CPU to it. Runs very frequently. Medium-Term Scheduler: Swaps processes out of memory to disk and later swaps them back in to relieve memory pressure and improve the process mix.

Explain the difference between Multiprogramming and Time-Sharing as objectives of process scheduling. Multiprogramming Objective: To maximize CPU utilization. The scheduler ensures the CPU is never idle by switching to a new process only when the current one blocks for I/O. Time-Sharing Objective: To maximize interactivity and response time. The scheduler uses a time quantum to rapidly preempt processes, allowing multiple users to interact with the system simultaneously without noticeable lag.

Explain why Context Switching is necessary, listing any three situations in which it occurs. Context Switching is necessary because a single CPU core can only execute one process at a time. To provide the illusion of multitasking, the OS must rapidly swap processes in and out, saving their state so they can resume exactly where they left off. Situations: A hardware interrupt occurs (e.g., a key is pressed). A process's time quantum expires in a Time-Sharing system. A process makes a blocking System Call (e.g., requesting to read a file).

Differentiate between a Single-threaded process and a Multi-threaded process, with one example of each. Single-Threaded Multi-Threaded Has only one path of execution. Has multiple concurrent paths of execution. If it blocks for I/O, the entire application halts. If one thread blocks, others continue executing. Ex: A basic Notepad application. Ex: A Web Browser (one thread downloads, another renders UI).

A process must first move from disk into main memory before it can begin execution, and later gets swapped out temporarily while waiting for I/O. Identify which schedulers are responsible for these two actions respectively, and briefly explain their roles. Long-Term Scheduler: Responsible for moving the process from the disk (job pool) into main memory to begin execution. It dictates the degree of multiprogramming. Medium-Term Scheduler: Responsible for swapping the process out temporarily to the disk when waiting for I/O, freeing up RAM for other processes, and swapping it back in later.

A process has Arrival Time = 0 and Burst Time = 8, but its execution actually starts at time = 3. Calculate its Response Time, and give one possible reason the process had to wait before starting. Response Time: Time of first CPU access - Arrival Time = 3 - 0 = 3 . Reason for waiting: The CPU was currently occupied by another process that either arrived earlier (FCFS) or had a higher priority/shorter burst time, so this process had to wait in the Ready Queue until the CPU became available.

Explain how a 'user thread' created for spell-check in a Word application actually gets executed by the CPU, given that the CPU can run only kernel threads. Describe the linking process step by step. The CPU hardware only knows about Kernel Threads . A User Thread (like spell-check) is created purely in user space by a thread library. To execute it, the library must map it to a Kernel Thread. The user library creates the spell-check thread. The library maps this thread to an available Kernel Thread using a multi-threading model (e.g., Many-to-One or Many-to-Many). The OS scheduler schedules that specific Kernel Thread onto a physical CPU core. When the Kernel Thread runs, it executes the code of the user thread mapped to it.

Explain User Threads and Kernel Threads in detail, listing the advantages and disadvantages of each. Type Advantages Disadvantages User Threads Very fast to create and switch (no OS trap required). Highly portable across different OSs. If one thread makes a blocking system call, the OS blocks the entire process (all threads halt). Cannot utilize multiprocessors. Kernel Threads If one thread blocks, the OS can schedule another. Can execute simultaneously on multiple CPU cores. Slow to create and manage because every operation requires a system call / mode switch.

Differentiate between the Long-Term Scheduler, Short-Term Scheduler, and Medium-Term Scheduler on the basis of their function, frequency of execution, and the queues they operate on. Scheduler Function Frequency Queues Operated On Long-Term Selects processes from disk and loads them into memory. Controls degree of multiprogramming. Low (runs infrequently, minutes/seconds). Job Queue → Ready Queue Short-Term Selects the next process to execute on the CPU. Very High (runs every few milliseconds). Ready Queue → CPU (Running) Medium-Term Swaps partially executed processes out to disk and back to free up RAM. Medium. Memory ↔ Swap Space (Disk)

Consider three processes: P1 (AT=0, BT=5), P2 (AT=1, BT=3), P3 (AT=2, BT=8). Compute the Completion Time, Turnaround Time, and Waiting Time using FCFS scheduling. Using First Come First Serve (FCFS) : P1 arrives at 0. Executes 0 to 5. CT = 5 . TAT = 5 - 0 = 5. WT = 5 - 5 = 0. P2 arrives at 1. Waits till 5. Executes 5 to 8. CT = 8 . TAT = 8 - 1 = 7. WT = 7 - 3 = 4. P3 arrives at 2. Waits till 8. Executes 8 to 16. CT = 16 . TAT = 16 - 2 = 14. WT = 14 - 8 = 6. Average Waiting Time: (0 + 4 + 6) / 3 = 3.33

In a multi-core system, a web browser remains responsive overall even when one tab freezes because of a heavy script running in it, while other tabs keep working normally. Using the concepts of processes, threads, and multithreading, explain why this happens and how a well-designed browser/OS achieves this behaviour. A modern browser uses a Multithreaded / Multiprocess architecture . Instead of running the entire browser as a single-threaded process, it assigns a separate thread (or entire process) to each tab. Because these are Kernel Threads (or separate processes), the OS CPU Scheduler manages them independently. If Tab A gets stuck in an infinite script loop, its specific thread maxes out one CPU core. However, the OS continues scheduling Tab B's thread onto a different core (or preempts Tab A to give Tab B time). Thus, the frozen tab does not block the UI or the other tabs.

A student's laptop feels slow to respond when opening a new file because too many background applications are competing for the CPU. Identify which CPU scheduling criterion is most affected in this situation, and suggest a suitable scheduling algorithm that would improve the system's responsiveness, justifying your choice. The criterion most affected is Response Time . Suggested Algorithm: Round Robin (RR) . Justification: If the laptop is using an algorithm like FCFS or non-preemptive priority, background tasks might hog the CPU for long continuous bursts, causing the UI to freeze. Round Robin preemptively slices CPU time (e.g., every 10ms) and distributes it evenly across all processes. This guarantees that the UI thread gets frequent access to the CPU, drastically improving interactive responsiveness, even if the total completion time (throughput) decreases slightly.

Critically compare FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Round Robin, and Priority Scheduling algorithms, and justify which algorithm would be most appropriate for (a) a batch processing system with no user interaction, and (b) an interactive time-sharing system used by multiple users. Give reasons for each choice. (a) Batch Processing System: SJF (Shortest Job First) is most appropriate. Without user interaction, we don't care about fast response times. SJF mathematically guarantees the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes, maximizing overall throughput and efficiency for heavy background workloads. (b) Interactive Time-Sharing System: Round Robin (RR) is most appropriate. Multiple users require the system to feel "alive" and responsive. RR guarantees that every user's process receives a CPU time slice frequently, ensuring low Response Time and high fairness, preventing any single heavy user from monopolizing the system.

Define Concurrency. Give one real-world example from everyday computer usage. Concurrency is the execution of multiple instruction sequences at the same time. It happens when multiple threads or processes make progress overlapping in time, either through rapid context switching (single-core) or true parallel execution (multi-core). Example: Downloading a file in a web browser while simultaneously scrolling through a webpage.

What is a Critical Section? A Critical Section is a specific segment of code in a process where shared resources (like shared memory, variables, or files) are accessed and modified. To prevent data corruption, no two processes can be executing their critical sections simultaneously.

Define an atomic operation. Why is it important for synchronization? An Atomic Operation is an operation that executes entirely as a single, indivisible step. Once it starts, it cannot be interrupted or preempted halfway through. Importance: It guarantees that shared variables (like locks or counters) are updated safely without race conditions caused by a mid-instruction context switch.

Differentiate between a Counting Semaphore and a Binary Semaphore. Binary Semaphore (Mutex): Can only take values 0 or 1. Used strictly to enforce mutual exclusion for a single critical section. Counting Semaphore: Can take any non-negative integer value. Used to control access to a resource pool with multiple identical instances (e.g., managing 5 available printers).

What is the difference between the wait() and signal() operations of a semaphore? wait() (or P/down): Decrements the semaphore value. If the value becomes negative (or reaches 0 in a binary semaphore), the calling process is blocked and placed in a waiting queue. signal() (or V/up): Increments the semaphore value. If there are processes blocked in the waiting queue, one is woken up and moved to the ready queue.

In the Bounded Buffer problem, the semaphore empty is initialized to n and full is initialized to 0. Explain what these two semaphores represent. empty = n: Represents the number of empty slots available in the buffer for the Producer to fill. full = 0: Represents the number of filled slots available in the buffer for the Consumer to read.

Explain the two models of Inter-Process Communication (IPC). Shared Memory: Two processes establish a region of shared RAM. They communicate by reading and writing to this shared region directly. Fast, but requires explicit synchronization (e.g., semaphores) by the programmer. Message Passing: Processes communicate by sending and receiving messages through the OS kernel. Slower (due to system calls), but safer and easier to use in distributed systems.

State and briefly explain the three requirements of a solution to the Critical-Section Problem. Mutual Exclusion: If process P1 is executing in its critical section, no other process can enter theirs. Progress: If no process is in the critical section and some processes want to enter, the selection of the next process cannot be postponed indefinitely. Bounded Waiting: There must be a limit on how many times other processes can enter the critical section after a process has requested entry.

Differentiate between the Shared Memory and Message Passing IPC models on the basis of speed, data copying, and OS involvement. Feature Shared Memory Message Passing OS Involvement Only during initial setup. Kernel involved in every send/receive operation. Data Copying No copying required (direct access). Data is copied from user space to kernel space, then back to user space. Speed Very Fast. Slower (due to constant system calls).

Explain why high-level statements like counter++ and counter-- are not safe in a concurrent environment, referring to their internal machine-level steps. A high-level statement like counter++ is not an atomic operation . At the machine level, it breaks down into three distinct instructions: Load counter from memory into a CPU register. Increment the register. Store the register back to memory. If a context switch occurs right after step 1 or 2, another process might load the old, stale value of counter . When both processes eventually complete step 3, one will overwrite the other's update, causing a Race Condition .

Compare Semaphores and Monitors. Semaphores Monitors Low-level integer variables with wait() and signal() operations. High-level abstraction provided by the programming language (e.g., synchronized in Java). Prone to programming errors (e.g., forgetting to signal). Safer, as the compiler automatically handles mutual exclusion. Can be distributed across multiple functions/files. Encapsulates shared variables and methods within a single construct.

In a library system, multiple students may read a book's catalog entry at the same time, but only one librarian should be allowed to update the entry at a time. Identify the classical synchronization problem this illustrates, and name the semaphores/variables used to solve it. This illustrates the Readers-Writers Problem . (Students = Readers, Librarian = Writer). Semaphores/Variables used: mutex (Binary Semaphore): Protects the readcount variable. wrt (Binary Semaphore): Ensures mutual exclusion for Writers. It is also used to block Writers when Readers are reading. readcount (Integer): Tracks exactly how many readers are currently reading.

Explain how Peterson's Solution uses the flag[] array and the turn variable together to satisfy Mutual Exclusion, Progress, and Bounded Waiting for two processes. Mutual Exclusion: P0 sets flag[0]=true and turn=1 . It only enters if flag[1]==false OR turn==0 . If P1 is inside, flag[1] is true and turn would be 1, so P0 is blocked. They cannot both enter. Progress: If P1 doesn't want to enter, flag[1] is false, so P0 can enter immediately without being indefinitely postponed. Bounded Waiting: When P0 exits, it sets flag[0]=false . This immediately allows P1 (who might be waiting) to enter. P0 cannot re-enter and starve P1 because P0 will set turn=1 upon re-requesting, forcing itself to wait for P1.

Explain the working of the Test-and-Set Lock hardware synchronization mechanism, and evaluate which requirements of the Critical-Section Problem it satisfies and which it does not. Test-and-Set is an atomic hardware instruction. It reads the current value of a boolean variable (lock) and instantly sets it to true, entirely without interruption. while (TestAndSet(&lock)) { // do nothing (spin wait) } // Critical Section lock = false; Evaluation: Mutual Exclusion: YES. Because it is atomic, only the first process to execute it will see false and proceed; all others will see true and get stuck in the while loop. Progress: YES. When the lock is released, a waiting process will immediately grab it. Bounded Waiting: NO. There is no queue. If multiple processes are spinning, the hardware might arbitrarily keep giving the lock to P1 over and over, starving P2.

A shared buffer of size 5 is used by a Producer and a Consumer, and currently holds 3 items. Using the semaphores mutex = 1, empty, and full as described in class, determine the current values of empty and full, and explain step-by-step (in terms of wait/signal calls) what happens when the Producer inserts one more item into the buffer. Since buffer size = 5 and it holds 3 items: full = 3 , and empty = 2 . Step-by-Step Insertion: Producer executes wait(empty) . empty decrements from 2 to 1. (Checks if there is space). Producer executes wait(mutex) . mutex becomes 0. (Locks the buffer for exclusive access). Producer inserts the new item into the buffer. Producer executes signal(mutex) . mutex becomes 1. (Unlocks the buffer). Producer executes signal(full) . full increments from 3 to 4. (Notifies the Consumer that a new item is available).

A hospital's patient database is read by many doctors at the same time but updated by only one nurse at a time; while a nurse is updating a record, no doctor should be able to read stale or partial data. Model this as the Readers–Writers problem: identify the semaphores/variables required (mutex, wrt, readcount), and explain the entry-section and exit-section logic for a reader process. Variables Required: mutex (initialized to 1): Protects the readcount variable. wrt (initialized to 1): The main lock for the database, preventing Writers from entering if anyone is inside. readcount (initialized to 0): Number of active doctors (readers). Reader Logic (Doctors): Entry Section: The doctor executes wait(mutex) to safely increment readcount . If this doctor is the very first reader ( readcount == 1 ), they execute wait(wrt) to lock out all nurses (writers). They then signal(mutex) to let other doctors in. Exit Section: The doctor executes wait(mutex) to safely decrement readcount . If they are the very last reader leaving ( readcount == 0 ), they execute signal(wrt) , finally unlocking the database so a waiting nurse can update it.

Five philosophers sit at a round table with five forks between them; deadlock occurs when all five pick up their left fork at the same time. Explain this deadlock scenario in detail, and describe any two solutions discussed in class (limiting participants, all-or-nothing approach, asymmetric solution) to prevent it. Deadlock Scenario: If all 5 philosophers execute wait(left_fork) simultaneously, they all grab one fork. When they execute wait(right_fork) , they find it's already held by their neighbour. They all wait infinitely for a right fork that will never be released (Circular Wait). Solutions: Limiting Participants: Allow at most 4 philosophers to sit at the 5-seat table. This guarantees at least one philosopher will have access to two forks, break the cycle, finish eating, and release their forks. Asymmetric Solution: Number the philosophers. Even-numbered philosophers must pick up their left fork first, while odd-numbered philosophers must pick up their right fork first. This breaks the circular wait condition.
